title: Ash coat rack with five pegs
subtitle: Seasoned wood: a wall-mounted coat rack with turned wooden pegs mortised into an ash back rail
excerpt: A five-peg coat rack in seasoned ash: a planed back rail with five short wooden pegs, each mortised into the rail and glued in place. The pegs are turned or commercially sourced Shaker-style pegs. The rail mounts to the wall with countersunk screws through the back. Functional, long-lasting, and finishes well with oil.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the mortised-peg coat rack construction; Shaker furniture illustrated manuals (public domain) for the peg rail design.

glossaryTerms.definition: A turned wooden peg with a rounded knob end and a tapered tenon, designed for insertion into a peg rail. The traditional Shaker furniture peg rail is one of the most widely copied functional furniture forms.
A rectangular hole cut into wood to receive a tenon. The peg tenons here are round, so the mortise is a bored hole rather than a chopped rectangle.

content.text: A five-peg coat rack follows the Shaker peg rail principle: a flat board back rail with evenly spaced

glued into bored holes. The pegs are either commercially turned (available from craft suppliers) or turned on a pole lathe if you have one. The board is planed flat, sanded, and finished with raw linseed oil before the pegs are inserted.

One seasoned ash board, 90 cm long, 10 cm wide, 22 mm thick. Five Shaker-style turned wooden pegs with 9 mm tenon diameter. Ash is the right timber for a coat rack, it is strong across the grain (the load of a full coat acts across the grain of the back rail at each peg point), and it is common, cheap, and planes well.
chisel and carpenter's mallet for any peg adjustment.
Cordless drill with 9 mm auger bit for the peg holes.

Plane the front face of the back rail flat and straight. Trim the ends square with the tenon saw. Rout or chamfer the top and bottom long edges with a light plane pass, one chamfering pass at 45 degrees removes the sharp arrises and gives a finished appearance.
Step 2: Mark and bore the peg holes

Mark five peg positions along the centre of the board face, equally spaced 16 cm apart, starting 13 cm from each end. Use the combination square to mark each position square across the board. At each mark, bore a 9 mm hole perpendicular to the board face, 15 mm deep, clamp the board firmly before drilling, and use a depth stop or tape on the drill bit to prevent going through.
Step 3: Mark and bore the wall fixing holes

Mark two fixing positions on the back face of the rail, 20 cm from each end. Bore 5 mm clearance holes through the board at each position. Countersink the holes on the back face so the screw heads sit flush. These are the fixing screws that go into the wall.

Test each peg tenon in its hole, it should be a friction fit, going in with hand pressure and not coming out without effort. Apply a small amount of wood glue to each peg tenon and push it firmly into its hole. The peg should stand at the correct angle (angled slightly upward, typically 5, 10 degrees). Wipe off any glue squeeze-out immediately. Leave to set for 24 hours before finishing.
Sand the rail to 240 grit and apply one coat of raw linseed oil. Allow to cure for two weeks before loading. RLO rags: always lay flat to dry.

attrs.symptom: A peg sits at the wrong angle after gluing, it points downward instead of level or upward
attrs.cause: The bore hole was drilled at a downward angle rather than perpendicular or slightly upward
attrs.fix: If the peg is still wet-glued, pull it out, clear the glue with a damp cloth, and re-drill the hole at the correct angle. If the glue has set, the easiest fix is to fit a new peg with a longer tenon that fills the existing hole plus a small additional rebore at the correct angle.
